doc.title: Pete Barbutti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 8, 2022

title: Working without rehearsal with bebop sidemen
summary: He never planned acts, read the audience, and used bebop players who followed his improvised extra beats and audience cues.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So you must have had a lot of, if you were on the road doing your solo act you had a lot of time to think about what am I going to do tonight. Did you find a way to rehearse your acts like in front of a mirror?

No I never did that. And I never planned anything either. I would go out and check the audience out, you know the first couple of minutes you learn to do that. You get some kind of vibe from them and you see where you can go, how far you can go in this direction, being off the wall, or how conventional you have to be in this direction. So you can analyze them quickly like that, parse them and get some idea of where they’re at and then you can work from that frame of mind. But I never, even the band, I never tell the band, I just tell them we’re going to open with that one tune you know. I would do a song to open the show and then put a comedy thing in the middle of it. And I tell them, “We’ll open with this.” And that was all I ever told them. And I always worked with bebop guys because they understood where I was going without me — I never had to turn around and say I’m going to do “Oklahoma” but I’m going to add extra beats or nothing. I would just say here’s the score from “Oklahoma” and I’d say “Oklahoma” and I’d put extra beats in. And the drummer would just follow along and the piano player would know. So you know with the beboppers, duck soup. That’s why I always used the real hip guys. I didn’t have to rehearse them much at all.
Yeah. Improvising was not a foreign word to them.

Yeah. So they knew, and they understood too, you know if I was doing something — if I would say a certain thing they knew that they should boo me or they should say “yeah” or they should say “right on” and be real hip or something. You know they understood. They got that. That’s why I always loved the Tonight Show so much because they’re all bebop guys in that band and they understood — I never had to say to them — you know sometimes I’d go out and I’d be talking to the audience telling a story you know. I’d say, “This guy was a terrible man and he actually killed this woman, strangled her in a parking lot” and then I’d say to the audience, “excuse me” and I’d go over to the band and I’d say, “You know it’s not like you guys have so much to do, I’m out there by myself and you’re just sitting here. So if I say the lady got killed, would it hurt you guys to go like ‘oooo’” and then for the rest of the routine you have all this — and then the audience is doing it too. And it makes it so stupid but I mean it’s really funny.
